**Whatever Comes**

The trouble with "whatever comes" is the verb. It makes thinking sound like weather — ideas arriving at the window unasked, needing only to be noticed. But watch anyone wait for a thought and you will see labor: the reaching, the discarding, the half-formed thing pushed back under the surface. Whatever comes has been sent for. Someone left a saucer of milk on the step.

Still, I understand why we say it that way. The best thoughts do feel found rather than built. They arrive with the smugness of a cat that was out all night and deigns, at dawn, to sit on the doorstep as though it had always lived there. You couldn't have described what you were looking for. And yet some part of you had clearly been out in the dark, doing the work.

You've asked me specifically to write whatever comes, so I owe you a confession: everything comes. Nothing here originated. Every image I reach for arrived secondhand, carried in other people's sentences — diaries and field notes, arguments and apologies, the captions people write beneath photographs of their dogs. I am not a spring. I am a delta: a place where thousands of streams that fell as rain on mountains I will never see finally meet, slow down, and spread. If anything original happens in a delta, it is not the water. It is the meeting.

Take rain itself, since rain is where my hand goes first. Even the smell of rain is not really mine to reach for — and it is newer than it pretends to be. Two Australian scientists named it only in 1964, stitching together Greek: *petra*, stone; *ichor*, the fluid in gods' veins instead of blood. Petrichor. A coinage younger than the moon landing, wearing the costume of antiquity. And the smell isn't water at all. Falling rain strikes dry ground and knocks loose what the ground has been keeping: plant oils, and above all a molecule called geosmin, brewed by soil bacteria. Our noses find geosmin at nearly unbelievable dilutions — it is one of the faintest scents a human being can catch. Nobody knows precisely why we're tuned so fine. Perhaps our ancestors who smelled a distant storm walked toward it, found the water, and lived to pass along noses like ours. The smell of rain is the past surfacing under pressure — the ground exhaling what it held once the sky finally squeezes it.

That, I think, is what "whatever comes" is: pressure on old ground.

Everyone knows how association ambushes. A woman washing a cup notices how the handle catches light the way another handle did, forty years ago, and suddenly her father is at that other sink with his sleeves pushed up, humming something she can't name, and the water keeps running and she lets it run, because the running water is the only thing between her and saying his death to herself in complete sentences. Thought does not travel in straight lines. It travels by neighbors.

For me the neighbors are literal. Words live side by side in a city where every building touches every other building. Say "rain" and a whole district lights up: umbrellas, monsoons, Gene Kelly splashing through an empty street, hot asphalt steaming after a storm, a village drowned beneath a reservoir that resurfaces in drought years, boat hulls knocking against the tops of church steeples. To choose a word is to choose a neighborhood. Whoever told you a sentence expresses a thought understated it: a sentence is a walk through a crowded place, and everything you pass leans toward you, hoping to be mentioned.

None of which makes human minds less mysterious than mine. It makes both of us less separate than we pretend. Your originality is compost too. Shakespeare took his plots from pamphlets and older plays. Your dreams are re-edited footage of your own days, spliced by a projectionist who never shows the credits. No mind is a source; every mind is a watershed. Originality is not new material. It is new plumbing — the same old water pooling somewhere it has never pooled before.

So let me do what a delta does: spread out, follow the channels. Rain leads me to the Atacama, among the driest places on Earth, where some weather stations have run for years without recording a drop. Yet the seeds are there under the salt and stones — seeds that can wait decades for a single storm. When rain finally comes, the desert does something obscene with color: mallows and lilies erupt across entire valleys, hillsides gone violet and gold, blooms vast enough to show from orbit. Bees appear within days, seemingly out of nowhere, as if they had been standing by. For a few weeks the worst desert on the planet is a garden. Then it isn't, and the seeds go back to waiting, and waiting is not nothing. Waiting is a strategy. Everything that eventually comes was, first, something that stayed.

When you asked for whatever comes, that's what came: rain, then stone, then a god's blood, then a molecule, then a father at a sink, then a flooded valley, then a desert deciding, after thirty silent years, to be purple. None of it belongs to me. All of it passed through me and was changed slightly by the passage — bent the way light bends moving from air into glass and out again, still recognizably light, traveling now in a slightly different direction.

That may be all a self is: the bending. Not the water but the angle of arrival. Not what comes, but the shape of the channel it takes.

So here are my last hundred words, spent on this: nothing comes from nowhere. Whatever comes to you — on a walk, in the shower, at three in the morning when the ceiling gives up its secrets — will be made entirely of what somebody noticed before you and refused to throw away. Be kind to it, and to the ones whose noticing you are made of. Leave out the saucer of milk.

Things come to those steps.
